Instability of periodic waves for the Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers equation with monostable source

Abstract.

In this paper, it is proved that the KdV-Burgers equation with a monostable source term of Fisher-KPP type has small-amplitude periodic traveling wave solutions with finite fundamental period. These solutions emerge from a supercritical local Hopf bifurcation around a critical value of the wave speed. Moreover, it is shown that these periodic waves are spectrally unstable as solutions to the PDE, that is, the Floquet (continuous) spectrum of the linearization around each periodic wave intersects the unstable half plane of complex values with positive real part. To that end, classical perturbation theory for linear operators is applied in order to prove that the spectrum of the linearized operator around the wave can be approximated by that of a constant coefficient operator around the zero solution, which intersects the unstable complex half plane.

Key words and phrases: 
KdV-Burgers-Fisher equation, periodic waves, Hopf bifurcation, Floquet spectrum, spectral instability
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
35Q53, 35B10, 35B35, 35P05, 47A75.

1. Introduction

The Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers (KdVB) equation,

ut+α​u​ux−μ​ux​x+β​ux​x​x=0,u_{t}+\alpha uu_{x}-\mu u_{xx}+\beta u_{xxx}=0,

with μ>0\mu>0, β>0\beta>0, was first derived by Su and Gardner [33] for a wide class of Galilean invariant physical systems under the weak nonlinearity and long wavelength approximations, resulting into a model equation which underlies a balance between both dispersive and dissipative effects. It has been used to describe the approximate behavior of many physical phenomena such as weakly nonlinear plasma waves with electron inertial effects [17], undular bores in shallow water [20], cascading processes in turbulence theory [30], wave propagation in an elastic tube filled with a viscous fluid [19], the flow of liquids containing gas bubbles [34], waves in electronegative plasma [13, 1] and the description of gravity waves in atmospheric dynamics [21], among many others. A combination of the (viscous) Burgers [8] and the Korteweg-de Vries [29] equations, the KdVB model is perhaps the simplest physically relevant scalar equation containing a nonlinear transport or convection term, u​uxuu_{x}, a dissipation or viscosity term, ux​xu_{xx}, and a dispersive term, ux​x​xu_{xxx}, into one single equation. In all the aforementioned applications, the study of traveling wave solutions is a fundamental issue. The literature on nonlinear wave propagation for the KdVB equation is very extensive and we do not pretend to make a review here. The reader is referred to the classical review paper by Jeffrey and Kakutani [18] and to the references cited therein.

In this paper, we consider the KdVB equation with a monostable source term, also known as the Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers-Fisher (KdVBF) equation [26],

ut+α​u​ux−μ​ux​x+β​ux​x​x=r​u​(1−u),u_{t}+\alpha uu_{x}-\mu u_{xx}+\beta u_{xxx}=ru(1-u), (1.1)

describing the dynamics of a real, scalar unknown quantity u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t), depending on space, x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, and time, t>0t>0, and where α,β,μ,r≥0\alpha,\beta,\mu,r\geq 0 are non-negative constants. Since we are interested in the interplay between dissipation, dispersion, nonlinear transport and reaction, we assume that all physical constants are positive, α,β,μ,r>0\alpha,\beta,\mu,r>0. Under this assumption and without loss of generality, we normalize the model by making the transformations

x→μβ​x,t→μ3β2​t,α→μ4β3​α,r→β2μ3​r,x\to\frac{\mu}{\beta}x,\quad t\to\frac{\mu^{3}}{\beta^{2}}t,\quad\alpha\to\frac{\mu^{4}}{\beta^{3}}\alpha,\quad r\to\frac{\beta^{2}}{\mu^{3}}r,

in order to recast equation (1.1) as

ut+α​u​ux+ux​x​x=ux​x+r​u​(1−u),u_{t}+\alpha uu_{x}+u_{xxx}=u_{xx}+ru(1-u), (1.2)

for some fixed constants α>0\alpha>0 and r>0r>0; this is the model equation that we work with for the rest of the paper.

The KdVBF equation (1.1) was recently introduced by Koçak [26], who proved the existence of traveling waves (such as solitons, kink and anti-kink waves) under the presence of the reaction term

f⁡(u)=r​u​(1−u),f(u)=ru(1-u),

also known as a logistic reaction function. This particular form of the reaction term was considered by Fisher [12] and by Kolomogorov, Petrovsky and Piskunov [28] in the context of reaction-diffusion equations modelling invasion fronts, and it is often used to model dynamics of populations with limited resources which saturate into a stable equilibrium point associated to an intrinsic carrying capacity (in this case, the equilibrium state u=1u=1). Although the nomenclature is not uniform, it is often known under the names of monostable, logistic or Fisher-KPP reaction term. It is one of the most widely used production mechanisms giving rise to wave propagation and determining their dynamics. Other studies have also considered the KdVB equation with sources: Gao [13], for instance, derived the KdVB equation with a linear reaction term (a damping source) in the study of waves in electronegative plasma. We conjecture that the KdVBF equation might be derived in the long wavelength and weakly nonlinear approximations from a physically significant system, albeit such derivation is, as far as we know, still unknown.

The purpose of this paper is to contribute to the analysis of nonlinear waves for the KdVBF equation (1.1). We study for the first time the problem of existence of periodic waves. Instead of applying the common methods based on exploiting symmetries, or on solving the differential profile equations on a case-by-case basis, we prove the existence of periodic waves via application of local bifurcation methods [35, 4, 3, 9]. Profiting from the presence of the unstable equilibrium point of the reaction function, we prove that a family of small-amplitude periodic waves emerges from a supercritical local Hopf bifurcation around a critical value of the wave speed; this is the first result of the paper, see Theorem 2.1 below. These waves have small amplitude and bounded fundamental period. The amplitudes are of order of the square root of the distance between the speed and the critical speed. The instability of the equilibrium point of the reaction is responsible for the existence of the waves and for the change of stability of the equilibrium point as the wave speed crosses the bifurcation critical value. Some numerical approximations illustrate the emergence of this family of waves.

Next, we study the stability of these bounded periodic waves as solutions to the nonlinear evolution equation (1.2). As it is customary, we first linearize the equation around each periodic wave and study the resulting spectral problem. In the case of periodic waves, the linearized operator has periodic coefficients, leading to the concept of the Floquet spectrum, see [23, 22, 14]. We then recast the problem of locating the continuous or Floquet spectrum as a point spectral problem on an appropriate periodic space via a Bloch-type transformation. Since the waves have small amplitude, we follow previous analyses [4, 3, 9, 27] and prove that the spectrum can be approximated by the spectrum of a constant coefficient operator around the zero solution. For that purpose, a key ingredient is to show that the perturbed problem encompasses relatively bounded perturbations. The analysis is based on recasting the spectral equations for the Bloch-type operators as a perturbation problem, where the perturbation parameter is precisely the distance between the speed and the critical speed. We then apply the classical perturbation theory for linear operators (cf. [24, 16]) to show that the unstable point eigenvalue of the unperturbed operator splits into neighboring curves of Floquet spectra of the underlying small amplitude waves, proving in this fashion the spectral instability result, which is the main result of the paper, see Theorem 4.1 below. Up to our knowledge, this is the first analysis of existence and stability properties of periodic waves for the KdVBF equation (1.2).

2. Small-amplitude periodic waves

This section is devoted to prove that small amplitude periodic wave solutions to equation (1.2) do exist. These waves emerge from a Hopf bifurcation thanks to the the presence of an unstable equilibrium point of the reaction function.

2.1. Existence of periodic waves

A periodic wave is a solution to (1.2) of the form

u⁡(x,t)=φ⁡(x−c​t),u(x,t)=\varphi(x-ct), (2.1)

where the profile function, φ=φ⁡(ξ)\varphi=\varphi(\xi), φ:ℝ→ℝ\varphi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}, is at least of class C3C^{3} and periodic, with fundamental period L>0L>0, that is, φ⁡(ξ+L)=φ⁡(ξ)\varphi(\xi+L)=\varphi(\xi) for all ξ∈ℝ\xi\in\mathbb{R}. Here ξ=x−c​t\xi=x-ct denotes the Galilean variable of translation, and c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} is the wave speed. Upon substitution of the ansatz (2.1) into (1.2) one obtains the differential profile equation,

−c​φ′+α​φ​φ′+φ′′′=φ′′+r​φ​(1−φ),-c\varphi^{\prime}+\alpha\varphi\varphi^{\prime}+\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime}=\varphi^{\prime\prime}+r\varphi(1-\varphi), (2.2)

where ′=d/dξ{}^{\prime}=d/d\xi.

Φ=(ϕ1ϕ2ϕ3):=(φφ′φ′′),\Phi=\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{1}\\ \phi_{2}\\ \phi_{3}\end{pmatrix}:=\begin{pmatrix}\varphi\\ \varphi^{\prime}\\ \varphi^{\prime\prime}\end{pmatrix},

Identifying the first component of each of these periodic orbits as a periodic traveling wave for equation (1.2), we have thus proved the following existence result.

Theorem 2.1 (existence of small amplitude periodic waves).

For any fixed parameter values r,α>0r,\alpha>0, there exist ϵ0>0\epsilon_{0}>0 sufficiently small and a critical speed value c0=−rc_{0}=-r such that the KdV-Burgers-Fisher equation (1.2) has a family of smooth periodic traveling wave solutions of the form u⁡(x,t)=φϵ​(x−c⁡(ϵ)​t)u(x,t)=\varphi^{\epsilon}(x-c(\epsilon)t), indexed by ϵ∈(0,ϵ0)\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_{0}), with fundamental period

Lϵ=2​πr+O⁡(ϵ),L_{\epsilon}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{r}}+O(\epsilon), (2.7)

and with amplitude growing like

|φϵ|,|(φϵ)′|=O⁡(ϵ).|\varphi^{\epsilon}|,|(\varphi^{\epsilon})^{\prime}|=O(\sqrt{\epsilon}). (2.8)

For any ϵ∈(0,ϵ0)\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_{0}), the speed of propagation is given by c⁡(ϵ)=−r+ϵc(\epsilon)=-r+\epsilon, and satisfies c⁡(ϵ)→c0c(\epsilon)\to c_{0} as ϵ→0+\epsilon\to 0^{+}. Finally, the periodic wave φϵ\varphi^{\epsilon} is unique up to translations, for each fixed ϵ∈(0,ϵ0)\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_{0}).

Remark 2.2.

From condition (2.6) and standard bifurcation theory, a unique curve of periodic orbits bifurcate into the region c⁡(ϵ)>c0=−rc(\epsilon)>c_{0}=-r. As a result, the linearization at the rest point P0P_{0} passes from having eigenvalues with Re​λ1>0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_{1}>0 and Re​λj<0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_{j}<0, j=2,3j=2,3 when c=−r+ϵc=-r+\epsilon with ϵ<0\epsilon<0, to a unstable hyperbolic focus with Re​λj>0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_{j}>0, j=1,2,3j=1,2,3, for c=−r+ϵc=-r+\epsilon with ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Hence, the change of qualitative behavior of the system corresponds to a supercritical Hopf bifurcation and the emerging periodic orbits for ϵ>0\epsilon>0 are stable. Of course, this notion of stable/unstable periodic orbit refers to the standard concept from dynamical systems theory: an orbit is stable as a solution to system (2.3) for a constant value of cc if any other nearby solution to the system with the same cc tends to the orbit under consideration. This definition of stability is completely unrelated to the concept of spectrally stable periodic wave, which refers to the dynamical stability of the traveling wave as a solution to the evolution PDE, see [4, 3] for further information and discussions. Actually, we shall prove that these orbits are spectrally unstable as periodic wave solutions to the KdVBF equation (1.2).

2.2. Numerical approximation

In order to illustrate the emergence of small amplitude periodic waves for the KdVBF equation (1.2), let us fix the physical parameters as r=α≡1r=\alpha\equiv 1. Then the dynamical system (2.3) in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} now reads

(ϕ1ϕ2ϕ3)′=(ϕ2ϕ3ϕ3+ϕ1​(1−ϕ1)−ϕ1​ϕ2+c⁡(ϵ)​ϕ2),\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{1}\\ \phi_{2}\\ \phi_{3}\end{pmatrix}^{\prime}=\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{2}\\ \phi_{3}\\ \phi_{3}+\phi_{1}(1-\phi_{1})-\phi_{1}\phi_{2}+c(\epsilon)\phi_{2}\end{pmatrix}, (2.9)

where the speed, or bifurcation parameter, is given by c⁡(ϵ)=c0+ϵ=−1+ϵc(\epsilon)=c_{0}+\epsilon=-1+\epsilon and ϵ\epsilon takes values in a neighborhood of zero. As before, ′=d/dξ{}^{\prime}=d/d\xi, where ξ=x−c⁡(ϵ)​t\xi=x-c(\epsilon)t denotes the translation variable, once the value of the speed has been fixed. Figure 1 shows the flow in the phase space of the solutions system (2.9) for c⁡(ϵ)=−1±ϵc(\epsilon)=-1\pm\epsilon with ϵ=0.001\epsilon=0.001. To that end, we used the standard tools provided by Mathematica©. For instance, Figure 1(a) depicts the flow when c=−1−0.001c=-1-0.001, that is, before the bifurcation occurs. Notice that the origin is a hyperbolic saddle with both stable and unstable eigendirections. Figure 1(b) shows the flow in phase space of the system (2.9) for c=−1+0.001c=-1+0.001, right after the supercritical Hopf bifurcation occurs. The unique, small-amplitude periodic orbit that emerges as a result of such bifurcation is represented in red color.

It is to be observed that the small periodic orbit appearing in Figure 1(b) is, in fact, a numerical approximation. For that purpose, we used the NDSolve package, in which a standard explicit Runge-Kutta method was implemented with an initial point given by (0,0.01,0)(0,0.01,0). Figure 2(a) shows a magnification of the flow in phase space for the speed value c=−1+0.001c=-1+0.001 (the same as in Figure 1(b)), together with the computed periodic orbit. Figure 2(b) contains the plot of the first component of the approximated periodic orbit, ϕ1\phi_{1}, as a function of the translation variable ξ=x−c⁡(ϵ)​t\xi=x-c(\epsilon)t.

3. The stability problem

In this section we make precise the notion of spectral stability of the periodic waves under consideration and exhibit its equivalence to computing the Floquet spectrum of the linearized operator around the wave.

3.1. Spectral stability

Fix a parameter value ϵ∈(0,ϵ0)\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_{0}) and consider the unique traveling wave solution to (1.2), u⁡(x,t)=φϵ​(x−c⁡(ϵ)​t)u(x,t)=\varphi^{\epsilon}(x-c(\epsilon)t), from Theorem 2.1. With a slight abuse of notation, let us make the transformation x↦x−c⁡(ϵ)​tx\mapsto x-c(\epsilon)t in order to rewrite equation (1.2) as

ut−c⁡(ϵ)​ux+α​u​ux+ux​x​x=ux​x+r​u​(1−u).u_{t}-c(\epsilon)u_{x}+\alpha uu_{x}+u_{xxx}=u_{xx}+ru(1-u). (3.1)

In other words, we recast the problem into a Galilean coordinate frame under which the profile φϵ=φϵ​(x)\varphi^{\epsilon}=\varphi^{\epsilon}(x) is now a stationary solution to (3.1) (thanks to equation (2.2)). Motivated by the notion of spatially localized, finite energy perturbations in the Galilean coordinate frame in which the periodic wave is stationary, let us consider solutions to (3.1) of the form

u⁡(x,t)=φϵ​(x)+eλ​t​v​(x),u(x,t)=\varphi^{\epsilon}(x)+e^{\lambda t}v(x),

where λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C} and v∈L2​(ℝ)v\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}). Upon substitution and using the profile equation (2.2), the spatial perturbation vv must be a solution to the following nonlinear equation

λ​v+α​v​vx+(α​φϵ​(x)−c⁡(ϵ))​vx+vx​x​x=vx​x+(r⁡(1−2​φϵ​(x))−α​(φϵ)′​(x))​v−r​φϵ​(x)​v2.\lambda v+\alpha vv_{x}+(\alpha\varphi^{\epsilon}(x)-c(\epsilon))v_{x}+v_{xxx}=v_{xx}+\big(r(1-2\varphi^{\epsilon}(x))-\alpha(\varphi^{\epsilon})^{\prime}(x)\big)v-r\varphi^{\epsilon}(x)v^{2}.

Linearizing last equation we obtain

λ​v=−vx​x​x+vx​x−(α​φϵ​(x)−c⁡(ϵ))​vx+(r⁡(1−2​φϵ​(x))−α​(φϵ)′​(x))​v,\lambda v=-v_{xxx}+v_{xx}-(\alpha\varphi^{\epsilon}(x)-c(\epsilon))v_{x}+\big(r(1-2\varphi^{\epsilon}(x))-\alpha(\varphi^{\epsilon})^{\prime}(x)\big)v,

that is, we arrive at the following spectral problem for the linearized operator around the periodic wave,

λ​v=ℒϵ​v,\lambda v={\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon}v, (3.2)

where, for each 0<ϵ<ϵ00<\epsilon<\epsilon_{0}, the linear operator ℒϵ{\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon} is defined as

{ℒϵ:L2​(ℝ)→L2​(ℝ),D⁡(ℒϵ)=H3​(ℝ),ℒϵ:=−∂x3+∂x2+a1ϵ(x)∂x+a0ϵ(x)Id,\left\{\begin{aligned} {\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon}&:L^{2}(\mathbb{R})\to L^{2}(\mathbb{R}),\\ D({\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon})&=H^{3}(\mathbb{R}),\\ {\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon}&:=-\partial_{x}^{3}+\partial_{x}^{2}+a_{1}^{\epsilon}(x)\partial_{x}+a_{0}^{\epsilon}(x)\mathrm{Id},\end{aligned}\right. (3.3)

with coefficients

a1ϵ​(x)\displaystyle a_{1}^{\epsilon}(x) :=c⁡(ϵ)−α​φϵ​(x),\displaystyle:=c(\epsilon)-\alpha\varphi^{\epsilon}(x), (3.4)
a0ϵ​(x)\displaystyle a_{0}^{\epsilon}(x) :=r⁡(1−2​φϵ​(x))−α​(φϵ)′​(x),\displaystyle:=r(1-2\varphi^{\epsilon}(x))-\alpha(\varphi^{\epsilon})^{\prime}(x),

for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. Since the periodic wave is smooth and LϵL_{\epsilon}-periodic, the coefficients ajϵa_{j}^{\epsilon}, j=0,1j=0,1, and their derivatives are smooth, bounded and LϵL_{\epsilon}-periodic. Notice that the operator ℒϵ{\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon} is densely defined in L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}), with domain D⁡(ℒϵ)=H3​(ℝ)D({\mathcal{L}}_{\epsilon})=H^{3}(\mathbb{R}). Moreover, in view that the coefficients clearly satisfy ajϵ∈W1,∞​(ℝ)a_{j}^{\epsilon}\in W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}), j=0,1j=0,1, from Lemma 3.1.2 in [23], p. 40, we conclude that ℒϵ{\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon} is a closed operator in L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}).

Let us now recall some definitions from classical spectral theory. Let ℒ:X→Y{\mathcal{L}}:X\to Y be a densely defined, closed, linear operator with domain D⁡(ℒ)⊆XD({\mathcal{L}})\subseteq X and X,YX,Y Banach spaces. The resolvent set of ℒ{\mathcal{L}}, denoted as ρ(ℒ)|X\rho({\mathcal{L}})_{|X}, is defined as the set of complex numbers λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C} such that ℒ−λ{\mathcal{L}}-\lambda is invertible and (ℒ−λ)−1({\mathcal{L}}-\lambda)^{-1} is a bounded operator. The complement of ρ(ℒ)|X\rho({\mathcal{L}})_{|X} is what we call the XX-spectrum of ℒ{\mathcal{L}} and we denote it as σ(ℒ)|X=ℂ\ρ(ℒ)|X\sigma({\mathcal{L}})_{|X}=\mathbb{C}\backslash\rho({\mathcal{L}})_{|X}. Any complex number, λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C}, is said to belong to the point spectrum, σpt(ℒ)|X\sigma_{\mathrm{\tiny{pt}}}({\mathcal{L}})_{|X}, if ℒ−λ{\mathcal{L}}-\lambda is a Fredholm operator with index equal to zero and non-trivial kernel. Also, λ\lambda belongs to the essential (or continuous, in the periodic case) spectrum, σess(ℒ)|X\sigma_{\mathrm{\tiny{ess}}}({\mathcal{L}})_{|X}, provided that either ℒ−λ{\mathcal{L}}-\lambda is not Fredholm or it is Fredholm with non-zero index. Clearly, both the point and essential spectra are subsets of σ(ℒ)|X\sigma({\mathcal{L}})_{|X}. Moreover, since the operator is closed then there holds σ(ℒ)|X=σpt(ℒ)|X∪σess(ℒ)|X\sigma({\mathcal{L}})_{|X}=\sigma_{\mathrm{\tiny{pt}}}({\mathcal{L}})_{|X}\cup\sigma_{\mathrm{\tiny{ess}}}({\mathcal{L}})_{|X}, see [24], p. 167. The point spectrum comprises discrete eigenvalues with finite (algebraic) multiplicity. The reader is referred to Kato [24] and Kapitula and Promislow [23] for further information.

Definition 3.1 (spectral stability).

The periodic traveling wave solution, φϵ\varphi^{\epsilon}, to (1.2) is spectrally stable if the L2L^{2}-spectrum of the linearized operator around the wave ℒϵ{\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon} satisfies

σ(ℒϵ)|L2⊂{λ∈ℂ:Reλ≤0}.\sigma({\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon})_{|L^{2}}\subset\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\,:\,\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda\leq 0\}.

Otherwise, we say that it is spectrally unstable.

Remark 3.2.

The choice of L2L^{2} as a base space is motivated by the notion of spatially localized, finite energy perturbations in the translation coordinate frame in which the wave is stationary.

3.2. The Floquet spectrum

Since the coefficients of the differential operator ℒϵ{\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon} are periodic, it is well known from Floquet theory that ℒϵ{\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon} has no L2L^{2}-point spectrum and that σ(ℒϵ)|L2=σess(ℒϵ)|L2\sigma({\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon})_{|L^{2}}=\sigma_{\mathrm{\tiny{ess}}}({\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon})_{|L^{2}} (see Lemma 3.3 in [22], or Lemma 59, p. 1487, in [11]). Moreover, it is possible to parametrize the essential spectrum in terms of Floquet multipliers of the form ei​θ∈𝕊1e^{i\theta}\in\mathbb{S}^{1}, θ∈ℝ\theta\in\mathbb{R} (mod 2​π2\pi). For each θ∈(−π,π]\theta\in(-\pi,\pi], let us denote σθ\sigma_{\theta} as the set of complex numbers λ\lambda for which there exists a bounded non-trivial solution v∈L∞​(ℝ)v\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) to the quasi-periodic problem

λ​v\displaystyle\lambda v =ℒϵ​v,\displaystyle={\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon}v, (3.5)
∂xjv⁡(Lϵ)\displaystyle\partial_{x}^{j}v(L_{\epsilon}) =ei​θ∂xjv(0),j=0,1,2.\displaystyle=e^{i\theta}\partial_{x}^{j}v(0),\qquad j=0,1,2.

The Floquet spectrum is defined as

σF:=⋃−π<θ≤πσθ.\sigma_{F}:=\!\!\bigcup_{-\pi<\theta\leq\pi}\sigma_{\theta}.

It turns out that the Floquet spectrum coincides with σ(ℒϵ)|L2\sigma({\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon})_{|L^{2}}.

Lemma 3.3 (Floquet characterization of the spectrum).

σ(ℒ)|L2=σF\sigma({\mathcal{L}})_{|L^{2}}=\sigma_{F}.

Proof.

See the proof of Proposition 3.4 in Jones et al. [22]. ∎

One advantage of this characterization is that the purely essential spectrum σ(ℒ)|L2\sigma({\mathcal{L}})_{|L^{2}} can be recast as the union of partial spectral σθ\sigma_{\theta}. Moreover, for each fixed θ\theta the set σθ\sigma_{\theta} is discrete because it is the zero set of an analytic function (see, e.g., [22], p. 4649). One can further remove the dependence on θ\theta of the boundary conditions in (3.5) and pose the problem in a proper periodic space independently of (but indexed by) θ\theta, by means of a Bloch-type transformation (cf. [23]). Indeed, let us define

For each ϵ∈(0,ϵ0)\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_{0}) the periodic wave φϵ\varphi^{\epsilon} is spectrally unstable if and only if there exists θ0∈(−π,π]\theta_{0}\in(-\pi,\pi] for which

4. Spectral instability

In this section we follow recent stability analyses of periodic waves (cf. [4, 3, 9, 27]) to prove our main result, pertaining to the spectral instability of the waves of Theorem 2.1.

Theorem 4.1 (spectral instability of small amplitude periodic waves).

There exists ϵ1∈(0,ϵ0]{\epsilon}_{1}\in(0,\epsilon_{0}] such that every small-amplitude periodic wave φϵ\varphi^{\epsilon} with ϵ∈(0,ϵ1)\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_{1}) from Theorem 2.1 is spectrally unstable, that is, the Floquet spectrum of the linearized operator around the wave intersects the unstable half plane, namely

σ(ℒϵ)|L2∩{λ∈ℂ:Reλ>0}≠∅.\sigma({\mathcal{L}}^{\epsilon})_{|L^{2}}\cap\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\,:\,\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda>0\}\neq\varnothing.

In order to prove Theorem 4.1, we first need to pose the spectral problem (3.7) for each operator in (3.8) as a spectral problem for a perturbed operator, where the perturbation parameter will depend on ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

4.2. A quick review of perturbation theory for linear operators

For completeness, in this section we briefly recall the basic perturbation theory for a family of linear operators of the form ℒ⁡(κ)=ℒ(0)+κ​ℒ(1)+κ2​ℒ(2)+…{\mathcal{L}}(\kappa)={\mathcal{L}}^{(0)}+\kappa{\mathcal{L}}^{(1)}+\kappa^{2}{\mathcal{L}}^{(2)}+\ldots, where κ\kappa is a complex parameter. The reader is referred to the classical books by Hislop and Sigal [16] (chapter 15) and Kato [24] (chapter VII) for more information. We describe the fundamental conditions under which an eigenvalue λ0\lambda_{0} of ℒ(0){\mathcal{L}}^{(0)} persists for κ\kappa in a neighborhood of the origin. Let us first recall the definition of an analytic family of type (A) (see [24], p. 375, or [16], §15.4).

Definition 4.4.

A family of linear closed operators ℒ⁡(κ):X→Y{\mathcal{L}}(\kappa):X\to Y, with X,YX,Y Banach spaces, defined for κ\kappa in an open complex domain B⊂ℂB\subset\mathbb{C} containing the origin, is said to be analytic of type (A) if the domains are independent of κ\kappa, that is, D⁡(ℒ⁡(κ))≡DD({\mathcal{L}}(\kappa))\equiv D for all κ∈B\kappa\in B, and the mapping κ↦ℒ⁡(κ)​u\kappa\mapsto{\mathcal{L}}(\kappa)u is analytic in κ∈B\kappa\in B for each u∈Du\in D. In that case, ℒ⁡(κ){\mathcal{L}}(\kappa) has a convergent Taylor expansion of the form

ℒ⁡(κ)​u=ℒ(0)​u+κ​ℒ(1)​u+κ2​ℒ(2)​u+…,{\mathcal{L}}(\kappa)u={\mathcal{L}}^{(0)}u+\kappa{\mathcal{L}}^{(1)}u+\kappa^{2}{\mathcal{L}}^{(2)}u+\ldots,

converging in a disk |κ|<R|\kappa|<R inside BB independent of uu for some radius R>0R>0. Here ℒ⁡(0)=ℒ(0){\mathcal{L}}(0)={\mathcal{L}}^{(0)} and ℒ(j):D⊂X→Y{\mathcal{L}}^{(j)}:D\subset X\to Y are linear operators for each j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N}.

The following result is the general stability theorem for discrete eigenvalues of analytic perturbations of a closed operator. Essentially it says that a discrete eigenvalue splits into several eigenvalue branches under a perturbation. These branches tend to the original discrete eigenvalue when the perturbation parameter goes to zero.

Theorem 4.5.

Let ℒ⁡(κ){\mathcal{L}}(\kappa) be an analytic family of type (A) about κ0=0\kappa_{0}=0. Let λ0\lambda_{0} be a discrete eigenvalue of ℒ(0)=ℒ⁡(0){\mathcal{L}}^{(0)}={\mathcal{L}}(0). Then there exist families λℓ​(κ)\lambda_{\ell}(\kappa), ℓ=1,…,q\ell=1,\ldots,q, of discrete eigenvalues of ℒ⁡(κ){\mathcal{L}}(\kappa) such that:

  • (i)

    λℓ​(0)=λ0\lambda_{\ell}(0)=\lambda_{0} for all ℓ=1,…,q,\ell=1,\ldots,q, and the total algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalues λℓ​(κ)\lambda_{\ell}(\kappa), ℓ=1,…,q,\ell=1,\ldots,q, is equal to the algebraic multiplicity of λ0\lambda_{0};

  • (ii)

    each family λℓ​(κ)\lambda_{\ell}(\kappa) is analytic in κ1/p\kappa^{1/p} for some positive integer p∈ℤ+p\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}, that is, each family has a Puiseux series expansion of the form

    λℓ​(κ)=λ0+β1​ωℓ​κ1/p+β2​ω2​ℓ​κ2/p+…,\lambda_{\ell}(\kappa)=\lambda_{0}+\beta_{1}\omega^{\ell}\kappa^{1/p}+\beta_{2}\omega^{2\ell}\kappa^{2/p}+\ldots,

    for some βj∈ℂ\beta_{j}\in\mathbb{C} and where ω=e2​π​i/p\omega=e^{2\pi i/p}, converging in a (possibly smaller) disk |κ|<R′≤R|\kappa|<R^{\prime}\leq R. In particular, the branches are continuous in κ\kappa near the origin and λℓ​(κ)→λ0\lambda_{\ell}(\kappa)\to\lambda_{0} when κ→0\kappa\to 0.

Proof.

See Theorem 15.11, p. 155 in [16]. There are no negative powers of κ1/p\kappa^{1/p} so that the branches are continuous at the origin, see Knopp [25]. ∎

In order to apply the previous perturbation result, let us first examine the perturbed spectral problem (4.3) for the Bloch operator with θ=0\theta=0, namely, to

λ~​w=(ℒ00+ε​ℒ01)​w,w∈Hper3​([0,π]),\widetilde{\lambda}w=({\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0}+\varepsilon{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{1})w,\quad\qquad w\in H^{3}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}([0,\pi]), (4.10)

and consider its complexification:

{ℒ~0​(κ):=ℒ00+κ​ℒ01,D​(ℒ~0​(κ))=Hper3​([0,π]),ℒ~0​(κ):Lper2​([0,π])→Lper2​([0,π]),\left\{\begin{aligned} \widetilde{{\mathcal{L}}}_{0}(\kappa)&:={\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0}+\kappa{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{1},\\ D(\widetilde{{\mathcal{L}}}_{0}(\kappa))&=H^{3}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}([0,\pi]),\\ \widetilde{{\mathcal{L}}}_{0}(\kappa)&:L^{2}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}([0,\pi])\to L^{2}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}([0,\pi]),\end{aligned}\right. Notice that the Bloch operators for θ=0\theta=0 are given by

{ℒ00:Lper2​([0,π])→Lper2​([0,π]),D⁡(ℒ00)=Hper3​([0,π]),ℒ00=−π3∂y3+L0π2∂y2+L02c0π∂y+L03rId,\left\{\begin{aligned} {\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0}&:L^{2}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}([0,\pi])\to L^{2}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}([0,\pi]),\\ D({\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0})&=H^{3}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}([0,\pi]),\\ {\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0}&=-\pi^{3}\partial_{y}^{3}+L_{0}\pi^{2}\partial_{y}^{2}+L_{0}^{2}c_{0}\pi\partial_{y}+L_{0}^{3}r\,\mathrm{Id},\end{aligned}\right. (4.12)

and

(4.13)

We start by making a straightforward observation.

Lemma 4.6.

The Bloch operator ℒ00{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0} has a real positive discrete eigenvalue, λ~0=r​L03>0\widetilde{\lambda}_{0}=rL_{0}^{3}>0, which is associated to the constant eigenfunction w0​(y)≡1/π∈Hper3​([0,π])w_{0}(y)\equiv 1/\sqrt{\pi}\in H^{3}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}([0,\pi]), with ‖w0‖Lper2=1\|w_{0}\|_{L^{2}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}}=1.

Follows from a direct computation, as ℒ00​w0=r​L03​w0{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0}w_{0}=rL_{0}^{3}w_{0}. Moreover, clearly w0∈Hper3​([0,π])w_{0}\in H^{3}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}([0,\pi]) and ‖w0‖Lper22=∫0π|w0​(y)|2​𝑑y=1\|w_{0}\|_{L^{2}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}}^{2}=\int_{0}^{\pi}|w_{0}(y)|^{2}\,dy=1. As we have already mentioned, all eigenvalues of the Bloch operators (3.8) are discrete. The lemma is proved. ∎

Next, we show that the family ℒ~0​(κ)\widetilde{{\mathcal{L}}}_{0}(\kappa) is an analytic family of type (A). This is a direct consequence of ℒ01{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{1} being ℒ00{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0}-bounded.

Lemma 4.7.

There exists ε^>0\hat{\varepsilon}>0 such that the family of operators (4.11) is an analytic family of type (A) for κ∈Bε^\kappa\in B_{\hat{\varepsilon}}.

Proof.

From Lemma 4.3, in the particular case with θ=0\theta=0 we already know that the operator ℒ01{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{1} is relatively bounded with respect to ℒ00{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0} on the space Lper2​([0,π])L^{2}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}([0,\pi]). Therefore, there exist a,b>0a,b>0 such that

‖ℒ01​u‖Lper2≤a​‖u‖Lper2+b​‖ℒ00​u‖Lper2,\|{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{1}u\|_{L^{2}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}}\leq a\|u\|_{L^{2}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}}+b\|{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0}u\|_{L^{2}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}},

for all u∈D⁡(ℒ00)=Hper3​([0,π])⊂D⁡(ℒ01)=Hper2​([0,π])u\in D({\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0})=H^{3}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}([0,\pi])\subset D({\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{1})=H^{2}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}([0,\pi]). Thus, we can apply Theorem VII-2.6 and Remark VII-2.7 in Kato [24], pp. 377-378, to conclude that there exists a radius ε^>0\hat{\varepsilon}>0 such that the family ℒ~0​(κ)=ℒ00+κ​ℒ01\widetilde{{\mathcal{L}}}_{0}(\kappa)={\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0}+\kappa{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{1} is analytic of type (A) for |κ|<ε^|\kappa|<\hat{\varepsilon} (in fact, ε^<b−1\hat{\varepsilon}<b^{-1}). ∎

After these preparations, we are able to apply perturbation theory for the family of linear operators.

Lemma 4.8.

There exist ε1>0\varepsilon_{1}>0 and families of discrete eigenvalues, λ~ℓ​(κ)\widetilde{\lambda}_{\ell}(\kappa), ℓ=1,…,q\ell=1,\ldots,q, of the operators ℒ~0​(κ)=ℒ00+κ​ℒ01\widetilde{{\mathcal{L}}}_{0}(\kappa)={\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0}+\kappa{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{1} for |κ|<ε1|\kappa|<\varepsilon_{1} such that λ~ℓ​(0)=λ~0=r​L03>0\widetilde{\lambda}_{\ell}(0)=\widetilde{\lambda}_{0}=rL_{0}^{3}>0. From Lemmata 4.7 and 4.6 we know that ℒ00+κ​ℒ01{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0}+\kappa{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{1} is an analytic family of type (A) for |κ|<ε^|\kappa|<\hat{\varepsilon} and that λ~0=r​L03>0\widetilde{\lambda}_{0}=rL_{0}^{3}>0 is a discrete eigenvalue of ℒ00{\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{0}. We now prove the main result of the paper.

4.3. Proof of Theorem 4.1

In view that ε=ϵ\varepsilon=\sqrt{\epsilon}, let us choose 0<ϵ1:=min⁡{ϵ0,ε12}0<\epsilon_{1}:=\min\{\epsilon_{0},\varepsilon_{1}^{2}\}. Hence, from Lemma 4.8 we conclude that there exists θ0=0∈(−π,π]\theta_{0}=0\in(-\pi,\pi] for which the spectrum of the perturbed Bloch operator with θ=0\theta=0 and ϵ∈(0,ϵ1)\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon_{1}) intersects the unstable half plane (in view that λ~0=r​L03>0\widetilde{\lambda}_{0}=rL_{0}^{3}>0):

σpt(ℒ0ϵ)|L2per∩{λ∈ℂ:Reλ>0}≠∅.\sigma_{\mathrm{\tiny{pt}}}({\mathcal{L}}_{0}^{\epsilon})_{|L^{2}_{\mathrm{\tiny{per}}}}\cap\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\,:\,\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda>0\}\neq\varnothing.

Therefore, from the spectral instability criterion stated in Proposition 3.4 we obtain the result. Notice that if we vary θ≈0\theta\approx 0 (within a small neighborhood of the origin), we obtain actual curves of Floquet spectrum that remain in a neighborhood of the unstable half plane. This completes the proof of Theorem 4.1. ∎

5. Discussion

In this paper, we have proved the existence of bounded periodic waves for the KdVBF equation (1.2). For that purpose we have verified that, for any fixed positive values of the physical parameters α>0\alpha>0 and r>0r>0, a family of small-amplitude and finite period waves emerges from a supercritical local Hopf bifurcation around a critical value of the wave speed given by c0=−rc_{0}=-r. To illustrate the emergence of the waves we conducted numerical approximations of both the waves and of the flow in phase space for fixed parameter values. In addition, we studied the stability of the family of periodic waves as solutions to the PDE. In particular, we proved that these waves are spectrally unstable or, in other words, that the Floquet spectrum of the linearized operator intersects the unstable complex half plane. Heuristically, this instability result has a direct interpretation: the small amplitude waves shrink to the zero equilibrium solution when the small parameter tends to zero, ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0, and the linearized operator around the wave tends (formally) to a constant coefficient linearized Bloch operator around the origin. The latter has a spectrum determined by a dispersion relation that intersects the unstable half plane thanks to the positive sign of the reaction term at the rest state. We then invoke the classical perturbation theory for linear operators to conclude.

This perturbative technique has been recently applied to study stability of small-amplitude waves for scalar viscous balance laws [4], scalar Hamiltonian equations [27], hyperbolic systems of balance laws [3] and scalar reaction-diffusion equations coupled to one ordinary differential equation [9]. This appears to be a general behavior and the method could be used to study the instability of small periodic waves arising in other contexts. In a recent contribution, Chen and Duan [10] found the conditions (in a unified framework) to prove the perturbation results on the related spectra for a large class of second order differential operators with asymptotically constant coefficients. Their result does not apply, however, to the KdVBF equation, which is of third order. From a technical viewpoint, it is to be noticed that we did not prove that the unstable eigenvalue of the unperturbed operator is simple or non-degenerate. Nonetheless, we directly applied perturbation theory for a higher multiplicity eigenvalue for which the perturbation eigenvalue branches can be represented by a Pusieux series which remain continuous in the limit. This allows us to conclude the result. This feature exhibits the flexibility of perturbation theory of linear operators as a technique to examine instabilities of approximated waves in general situations. Finally, the instability results of the present study may serve as the theoretical basis to demonstrate the orbital (nonlinear) instability of the waves under consideration, as it happens in many other physical systems and model equations such as the KdV equation [31], viscous balance laws [2], the critical KdV and NLS models [6], KdV systems [5], and for general dispersive models [7], just to mention a few.
